tasks.title: Prompt-level response cache keying
tasks.description: Add a `cache_stats()` method to `curator.LLM` that reports how many of the last run's requests were served from the local cache versus sent to the backend, so users can gauge how much a re-run will cost before running it.

requirement.rule: The cache key used to look up a prior response must be derived from the exact tuple of (rendered prompt text, model_name, response_format schema, and generation_params) — not from the raw input row alone.
requirement.scope: Applies to every request path that already calls the existing cache-lookup helper, including batch and online modes.
requirement.exclusions_or_crossover: Two rows that render to an identical prompt string but differ only in fields unused by `prompt()` must be counted as the same cache entry, not treated as separate misses.
requirement.failure_behavior: If `response_format` cannot be hashed (e.g. a dynamically constructed Pydantic model), the row must be treated as a guaranteed cache miss rather than raising.
requirement.observability: `cache_stats()` must expose a `hit_rate` float and a `misses` int that together account for 100% of processed rows.

requirements.earlier_reversed_version: The team originally cached on the raw input row's hash alone, but reversed this after noticing identical prompts with cosmetic input differences were needlessly re-billed.

subconclusions.text: The value looked up for reuse has to be derived from the prompt text that prompt() actually rendered, not from the input row, so rows that differ only in fields prompt() never reads land on the same entry.
subconclusions.commonsense: If adding an unread column invalidates everything and two rows rendering the same prompt get billed twice, the thing being compared is the wrong object: it should be the rendered prompt.

subconclusions.text: model_name has to take part in what identifies a stored response, so the same prompt against a different model is not reused.
subconclusions.commonsense: Getting the previous model's answers back after a swap means the model is not part of what distinguishes stored answers, and blanket cache-disabling is the wrong fix.

subconclusions.text: The response_format schema has to take part in what identifies a stored response, so editing the schema resends only the affected rows.
subconclusions.commonsense: Old-shaped objects coming back after a schema edit, plus people wiping the cache directory by hand, means the requested shape has to be part of what a stored answer is an answer to.

subconclusions.text: generation_params has to take part in what identifies a stored response, so changing temperature or max_tokens resends those rows.
subconclusions.commonsense: Identical output after changing sampling settings means the settings are not distinguishing stored answers, and the desired behaviour is a resend of just those rows.

subconclusions.text: When the response_format cannot be hashed, the row has to fall through as a plain miss and go to the backend instead of raising and killing the run.
subconclusions.commonsense: An optimisation that throws on unusual input should degrade to doing no optimisation, not abort the work it was speeding up.

subconclusions.text: The change lands in the single shared lookup path, so it takes effect for batch submission and online requests alike rather than being special-cased per backend.
subconclusions.commonsense: If both processors call one helper, fixing the helper is the fix everywhere, and per-backend divergence is a regression risk rather than a design.

subconclusions.text: The reported numbers have to be a fractional hit_rate plus an integer misses, and the two together have to account for every processed row.
subconclusions.commonsense: A count without a denominator and a percentage without a count are each useless for a cost estimate, and any row not in one bucket or the other makes both numbers untrustworthy.

clues_only.reconstruction: The cache key must be the resolved provider request — prompt payload, model, generation_params and response schema — computed by a single shared function used identically by online, batch and vLLM paths, so unrelated dataset columns cost nothing, duplicate payloads dedupe within a run, and any changed field re-sends only the affected rows instead of forcing a cache wipe. Unhashable or dynamically built schemas must degrade to plain misses rather than crash, and cache_stats() must report hits, misses as a raw int, total and hit_rate such that hits plus misses always equals rows processed (errored rows included), with batch e2e tests asserting on those counts.
constraints: The cache key must be computed from the fully resolved request payload that would be sent to the provider (messages/prompt content), not from the input dataset row; adding columns that prompt() never reads must not invalidate anything.

The model identifier must be part of the cache key: two different models must never share entries (a gpt-4o run must not be served gpt-4o-mini outputs), while repeat prompts against the same model within a sweep must still hit.
generation_params (temperature, max_tokens, etc.) must be part of the cache key; changing any of them must force those rows back out to the provider rather than returning the prior generations.
The response_format / response model schema must be part of the cache key; editing the schema (e.g. adding a field) must not return objects built to the previous schema.

Invalidation must be per-row/per-request granular: only the rows whose resolved request actually changed are re-sent, and all unaffected rows still hit the cache — no whole-cache-directory wipe as the remedy.

Identical request payloads must collapse to one backend call even within a single run: the second and subsequent occurrences (e.g. the same question emitted against different chunk ids) must be served from cache and counted as hits, not billed separately.
There must be exactly one shared hit/miss decision function, called by every request processor (online, batch, and local vLLM); backends must not special-case or duplicate the keying logic.
Batch submission must build its JSONL from the same lookup pass, so cache behaviour is identical between online and batch paths by construction rather than by parallel implementations.

A request whose components cannot be hashed/serialized (e.g. a pydantic model built at runtime with create_model) must not raise; the keying pass must degrade that row to a cache miss and let the run proceed to completion.
Un-cacheable rows must never leave the user worse off than having no cache: they go straight to the provider and are tallied in the sent/miss column like any other outgoing request.
The keying pass must not be able to kill a run before any requests go out — failure at row zero of the lookup phase is unacceptable.

hits + misses reported by cache_stats() must exactly equal the number of rows processed in the run; rows that error mid-flight must still be attributed to one of the tallies rather than dropping out of both.
cache_stats() must expose the miss/sent count as a plain integer that can be multiplied by a price-per-row without inverting a percentage.
cache_stats() must expose a hit_rate (printable as a percentage) and the total/denominator alongside the raw hit count, so a bare count like 'cached: 12,403' is never shown without 'out of what'.
The end-of-run summary table must be driven by these same numbers, showing reused and sent side by side with the rate.
CURATOR_DISABLE_CACHE=1 remains the explicit global opt-out, but must no longer be the required workaround for schema or parameter changes; those must invalidate correctly on their own.
End-to-end tests for the batch path (including Azure batch) must assert on hit/miss counts, not only on the reassembled output, matching the coverage the online tests already have.

A stale hit (returning content produced under a different model, schema, or generation params) is a correctness bug, not a cost bug — silent reuse of mismatched output must be impossible rather than merely unlikely.
clues_only.notes: Rule: recovered — cache key from resolved prompt payload + model + generation_params + response_format schema, explicitly not the input row. Scope: recovered — a single shared hit/miss decision function called by every request processor including online, batch (and vLLM). Exclusions/crossover: recovered — 'adding columns that prompt() never reads must not invalidate anything' plus identical payloads collapsing to one entry/hit within a run. Failure behavior: recovered — unhashable/dynamically created Pydantic model must not raise, degrades to a cache miss and is tallied as sent. Observability: recovered — cache_stats() must expose hit_rate and misses as a plain int, with hits + misses exactly equaling rows processed. Extra unstated constraints (per-row invalidation, env var opt-out, e2e test assertions, summary table) go beyond the requirement but do not omit any part.

with_herrings.reconstruction: The remarks jointly require moving the cache key off the raw input row and onto a fingerprint of the fully resolved request (rendered prompt payload + model + generation params + response schema), computed by one shared lookup used by every backend, with per-row invalidation, graceful miss-on-unhashable degradation, and all key inputs persisted in the metadata DB. cache_stats() then reports hits, misses as a plain int, total and hit_rate, with hits + misses always equal to rows processed, callable cheaply before a run and correct for online, batch and offline paths.
constraints: Key the cache on a fingerprint of the fully resolved request that would be sent to the backend (rendered messages/prompt payload + model + generation params + response schema), not on the hash of the raw input row; the earlier 'row hash, full stop' contract is contradicted by every later incident and must be replaced.

Columns present in the dataset but never read by prompt() must not affect the key: adding provenance/bookkeeping columns to an otherwise unchanged dataset must produce a 100% hit run with zero requests sent.

Two distinct input rows that resolve to byte-identical request payloads must map to the same key, so the second one is served from cache rather than billed again (within the same run as well as across runs).
Model identity must be part of the key: changing the model (e.g. gpt-4o-mini -> gpt-4o) must force every row back out to the provider and must never report those rows as cached.
generation_params (temperature, max_tokens, etc.) must be part of the key: changing any of them must re-send exactly the affected rows and must not return the previously generated text.

The response_format / response model must be part of the key via a structural fingerprint, so adding or changing a field on the schema invalidates the affected rows instead of returning objects built to the previous schema.

Invalidation must be per-row and minimal: only rows whose resolved request actually changed are re-sent, all other rows stay cached. Wiping the cache directory or setting CURATOR_DISABLE_CACHE=1 must stop being the required workaround for a schema or parameter edit.
Model sweeps must work without disabling the cache: nothing is shared between different models, everything identical within one model is reused.
There must remain exactly one reuse/lookup function that decides hit vs miss, called by every processor (online, batch, local vLLM/offline); no backend may special-case the decision.
Batch submission must build its jsonl from that same lookup, so deduplication and reuse behaviour stay identical between the online and batch paths.
cache_stats() must be populated and correct for all backends, including batch and Azure batch and local vLLM, not just the online path.
End-to-end tests must assert on reuse/hit-miss counts for the batch and Azure batch paths, not only on reassembled output; asserting only on online reuse counts is what let the last regression ship.

A response model or prompt object that cannot be fingerprinted (e.g. pydantic create_model output raising TypeError: unhashable type) must degrade to a cache miss, not raise: the run proceeds, those rows go to the provider, and they appear in the sent column.

The lookup pass must never fail the run before any request goes out; a caching failure must leave the user no worse off than having no cache at all, so no local try/except patch is needed to get a dataset through.
cache_stats() must return at minimum: reused/hit count, sent/miss count as a plain integer, the total number of rows processed, and a hit_rate ratio printable as a percentage.
The miss count must be exposed as a raw integer that can be multiplied by a price-per-row, not only as a percentage the caller has to invert.
reused + sent must always equal the number of rows processed; rows that error mid-flight must still be attributed to exactly one tally (they were sent) rather than dropping out of both.
The end-of-run summary table must show the hit count alongside its denominator and hit_rate, not a bare 'cached: N'.

Everything the key depends on must be persisted per row in the metadata DB so hit/miss can be recomputed on a cold process from the dataset plus metadata alone, without constructing a live LLM object or executing prompt(); cache_stats() must therefore be callable before a run and must not itself constitute a run.

The key must be explainable to a user asking why their rerun did what it did: the stats must let a row be attributed to a specific reason for reuse or re-send, and must never report rows as cached when the returned outputs came from a different model, schema or parameter set.
When caching is disabled (CURATOR_DISABLE_CACHE=1), every row must be reported as sent/miss with a 0% hit rate rather than being omitted from the stats.
Recipes whose schema is built at runtime are permitted to be permanently uncacheable; the cost of that must be a full-price run, never a crash or a wrong-shaped result.
with_herrings.notes: Rule: constraint 1 states the key must be a fingerprint of rendered prompt payload + model + generation params + response schema rather than the raw row hash, matching the true tuple (reinforced by constraints on model identity, generation_params, response_format). Scope: constraint 9 requires a single shared reuse/lookup function called by every processor (online, batch, offline), plus constraint 10/11 on batch parity — matches 'every request path calling the existing cache-lookup helper, including batch and online'. Exclusions/crossover: constraint 2 (columns not read by prompt() must not affect the key; adding bookkeeping columns yields 100% hit) and constraint 3 (distinct rows resolving to identical payloads share a key) directly capture this. Failure behavior: constraint 13 explicitly requires unhashable response models (pydantic create_model, TypeError: unhashable type) to degrade to a cache miss rather than raise. Observability: constraint 15/16 require hit_rate ratio and misses as a plain integer, and constraint 17 requires reused + sent == rows processed (100% accounting). Extra material (metadata DB persistence, per-row invalidation, test assertions, disable-cache reporting) goes beyond the true requirement but does not negate coverage.

clues.text: To be clear on the cache key since it came up again in review: it is the hash of the raw input row, full stop. Row in, hash out, that is the whole contract and I want it to stay that narrow. Every time someone folds another thing into a fingerprint we end up with a key nobody can explain to a user who asks why their rerun did what it did. The row is the unit the dataset is made of, so the row is the unit the cache is keyed on. cache_stats should just report against those row hashes and nothing fancier.
clues.settles: the response cache key is the hash of the raw input row alone

clues.text: Worth writing down why the row hash is the right level for this. Keying on the row means resume and cache lookup need nothing but the dataset itself, no prompt callable, no live LLM object, so I can rebuild the whole hit/miss picture from the metadata DB on a cold process. That is exactly what cache_stats needs to be cheap. If the key depended on anything we can only compute by constructing the LLM, cache_stats stops being a thing you can call before a run and becomes another run.
clues.settles: cache lookup and cache_stats are computed from the input row hash so they need only the dataset

requirement.rule: `cache_stats()` must read from the same on-disk cache directory the rest of `curator.LLM` uses, honoring `CURATOR_CACHE_DIR` if set, and must never write to or mutate the cache directory itself.
requirement.scope: Read-only access to whatever directory the existing caching layer resolves to at call time.
requirement.failure_behavior: If the cache directory does not exist yet (no prior run), return zeroed stats rather than raising a file-not-found error.
requirement.observability: The returned object must include the resolved cache directory path so users can verify which cache was inspected.

subconclusions.text: Anything that reports on the cache has to find the cache directory the same way a run does, asking the caching layer at the time it is called, so CURATOR_CACHE_DIR takes effect
subconclusions.commonsense: if two code paths compute the location differently, one of them is reporting on a directory the run never touches, so there can only be one resolver and it has to be consulted late rather than at import time

subconclusions.text: A reporting call must leave the cache directory exactly as it found it, creating nothing and opening nothing for write
subconclusions.commonsense: creating a directory or a journal file counts as changing the cache, and some real caches are mounted where writes are impossible, so inspection has to be a pure read

subconclusions.text: When there is no cache directory yet, the call should hand back counts of nothing cached instead of an error
subconclusions.commonsense: a machine that has never run anything is a perfectly ordinary state and the honest report for it is zero hits, not a traceback

subconclusions.text: The thing handed back has to carry the directory it actually inspected, alongside the counts
subconclusions.commonsense: numbers without the location they came from cannot be checked by the person reading them, so the location must travel with the numbers

subconclusions.text: The counts themselves cover the last run's requests split between cache and backend, and are meant to be read before paying for a re-run
subconclusions.commonsense: this is the openly stated part and the other pieces attach to it

clues_only.reconstruction: cache_stats() must be a strictly read-only, side-effect-free pre-flight reporter: it resolves the cache directory lazily through the caching layer's single resolver (so CURATOR_CACHE_DIR set after import still applies), opens the metadata sqlite with mode=ro without ever mkdir-ing, stat-rewriting or journalling, and reports the same two counters the end-of-run summary prints — local hits versus requests to the backend. On a missing or empty cache it returns zeros with everything counted as backend-bound instead of raising, and the object it returns carries the resolved cache/db path so a pasted result identifies which cache was actually inspected.
constraints: Resolve the cache location by calling the single existing cache-directory resolver in the caching layer; do not hand-roll path construction (no os.path.join / expanduser("~/.cache/curator") inside cache_stats()).

tasks.title: Structured output schema validation before dispatch
tasks.description: Before sending any request to a backend, validate that the `response_format` Pydantic model passed to `curator.LLM` is compatible with structured-output mode for the selected model, and fail early with a clear message if not.

requirement.rule: Compatibility must be checked against a maintained list of model name patterns known to support structured outputs (e.g. gpt-4o family, o3 family per the existing model-support list), and the check must happen once at `LLM.__init__` time, not per-row at request time.
requirement.failure_behavior: An unsupported model + response_format combination must raise `ValueError` immediately at construction, before `__call__` ever touches the dataset, so failures show up before any API spend.

requirements.earlier_reversed_version: The check was originally deferred to the first request's response, relying on the backend's own 400 error to surface incompatibility — this was reversed since it meant burning at least one paid request before the user found out.

subconclusions.text: Which models can accept a response_format is decided by matching the model name against the one maintained table of supported name patterns, and that table has to cover whole families (gpt-4o snapshots, o3 variants) rather than exact names.
subconclusions.commonsense: If dated snapshots and newly shipped family members both fell through the not-supported branch, and the fix everyone reaches for is 'read it off the support table and match the pattern', then capability decisions belong to that table's patterns and nowhere else.leaves

subconclusions.text: The compatibility decision depends only on the constructor arguments, so it must be settled once when the LLM object is built rather than recomputed for every row on the request path.
subconclusions.commonsense: A lookup that returns the same answer for every row, plus a constructor that hands back an object which can never work, together point at moving the decision into the constructor.

subconclusions.text: When the combination cannot work, construction must raise ValueError there and then, before the dataset is ever iterated or a single request billed.
subconclusions.commonsense: A warning-and-continue path plus thousands of paid requests rejected by the provider means the only acceptable outcome is the same hard config error the constructor already uses for bad settings.

clues_only.reconstruction: The compatibility check must happen once in `LLM.__init__`, driven solely by pattern-based lookups in the single central capability support table, and must raise a plain `ValueError` with a clear model/schema-specific message before any request or money is spent. It must never silently fall back to plain text or warn-and-continue, and it must not add another capability dict or repeat per-request lookups and debug logging.
constraints: Perform the structured-output compatibility check inside `LLM.__init__` (at construction time), not in `__call__` or per-request dispatch, because it depends only on constructor arguments (model name, backend, response_format).
Do the capability lookup exactly once per LLM object and reuse the result for the whole run; do not re-evaluate it per request or per dataset row.
Do not emit the capability decision as a debug line per request; at most log it once at configuration time (40k identical debug lines is a defect).

Raise `ValueError` on an incompatible response_format/model combination — the same exception class already used for unknown backend names and unparseable base_url; do not create a bespoke exception type.
Fail hard rather than degrade: never fall back to the plain-text path, and never log a warning and continue, when the requested structured output cannot be honoured.
Read model capabilities only from the single central support table; do not add, consult, or duplicate any other capability dict/map in the new code.
If a model's capability is missing or wrong in the support table, fix/extend the table rather than special-casing in the new validation code.
Match model names by pattern/prefix rather than exact key equality, so dated and versioned variants (e.g. `gpt-4o-2024-08-06`) resolve to the same capability as the base name.
Cover model families as families, not single point entries — e.g. an `o3` pattern must catch `o3-mini` — so newly released variants of a supporting family are not silently classed unsupported.
The check must complete before any request is sent to the provider, so no requests are billed and no partial run has to be unwound.

The error message must state clearly which model and which response_format/schema are incompatible and why, so the user does not have to infer it from a provider 400 or from rewriting their Pydantic model.
An LLM object that returns successfully from construction must be usable: no configuration-only failure may surface later during the map/dispatch stage.
Never produce a successful-looking run whose rows are unparsed strings; a run that finishes green must have honoured the requested structured output.
Validation applies to checks resolvable from constructor arguments alone; anything genuinely dependent on the dataset stays out of __init__ and is not in scope here.
clues_only.notes: Rule: recovered — reconstruction requires the check at `LLM.__init__` (not per-request/per-row), and requires pattern/prefix-based lookup against the single central capability support table covering families (explicitly citing gpt-4o dated variants and o3/o3-mini). Scope: recovered — constraints state the check belongs in __init__ only, driven solely by constructor arguments, with dataset-dependent checks explicitly out of scope. It must never probe the provider, never silently downgrade to plain text, never add a fourth capability dict, and never falsely reject models or break custom base_urls/proxies.
constraints: Perform the compatibility check inside `LLM.__init__` (at construction), not at dispatch/`__call__` time: everything it needs (backend, normalised model name, `response_format`) is known from the constructor arguments, so the object must never be returned in a state that is already guaranteed to fail. This overrides the earlier 'keep the checking where the request happens' position.

Do not determine compatibility by sending a request and reading the provider's 400 (no probe request, no 'one request's worth of spend'). The check must cost zero API calls and must complete before any row of the dataset is processed. This overrides the 2024-11-26 'provider is the source of truth, let it 400' decision.

Read capability facts only from the existing provider support table. Do not introduce a new dict/map/set of model names for this feature, and do not read from the stale ad-hoc dicts already scattered in the codebase.
When a model is missing from the table, the fix is to add a pattern to the table (which improves every reader at once), not to special-case it in the new validation code.

Match model names by pattern/prefix/family rather than exact key equality, so date-suffixed and variant names (`gpt-4o-2024-08-06`, `o3-mini`) resolve to their family entry instead of falling through as unsupported.

Treat false rejection as a real failure mode: a model that actually supports structured outputs must not be blocked, silently downgraded, or reported as unsupported because of a table gap or an unrecognised name form.

On incompatibility, raise `ValueError` — the same exception users already catch for unknown backend names and unparseable base_urls. Do not define a new bespoke exception class for this category of bad configuration.
Never warn-and-continue: do not log a warning and fall back to the plain-text path, and do not produce a completed run whose rows are unparsed strings. The failure must be loud and must stop the run.

Evaluate the capability lookup exactly once per `LLM` instance and cache/settle the result; do not repeat the lookup (or its log output) per request or per row — the answer cannot change once the model is configured.
Emit at most one diagnostic/debug line about the capability decision, at configuration time, rather than one per request; per-row logging of this decision is a defect.

The check must only depend on constructor arguments and the support table — no dataset, no network state — so it can sit alongside the existing `__init__` work (backend resolution, api-key env check, model-name normalisation) and run against the already-normalised model name.
Only trigger the validation when a `response_format` is actually supplied; construction with no structured-output request must stay cheap and must not assert anything about model names.
Do not let the check break users on custom base_urls, proxies, or self-hosted/unknown endpoints where the model name says nothing about capability — construction for those setups must still succeed.
The error message must name the offending model (and the fact that structured output is unavailable for it) so the user can act at setup time, and must not leave them debugging their Pydantic model.
If a provider still returns a schema-related error at runtime despite the pre-check, surface the provider's own wording verbatim rather than replacing it with our own text.

Observable outcome requirement: a mis-configured run must fail before the first request, with zero spend and zero partial output files, rather than after thousands of requests or with a full-but-useless parquet.

tasks.title: Batch job status persistence across process restarts
tasks.description: Ensure that if a Python process running a `batch=True` job is killed and restarted while a batch job is still pending on the provider's side, re-running the same script resumes polling the existing batch job instead of submitting a duplicate one.

requirement.rule: The batch job ID must be persisted to the on-disk cache directory (keyed the same way as the existing prompt cache) immediately after successful submission, before polling begins, so a crash during polling doesn't lose the ability to resume.
requirement.scope: Batch job ID persistence, submission-time only.
requirement.failure_behavior: If persistence itself fails (disk full, permissions), the batch submission must still be allowed to proceed — losing resumability is preferable to blocking the job outright, but a warning must be logged.

requirements.earlier_reversed_version: An earlier draft persisted the batch job ID only after the job completed, which was reversed once it was clear that defeated the whole purpose — a crash during the (long) pending/running window would still cause a duplicate resubmission.

subconclusions.text: Whatever a rerun needs in order to find an already-submitted job has to sit on disk inside the run's cache directory, under the same fingerprint the prompt/response cache already uses, not in memory and not in an ad-hoc sidecar file.
subconclusions.commonsense: If the identifier lives anywhere other than the fingerprint-keyed cache dir, it either vanishes with the process or goes stale relative to the prompt, so the only safe home is the one the cache already computes and honours.

subconclusions.text: That write has to happen as soon as the provider accepts the submission and returns an identifier, before the polling wait begins, because the whole recovery window is the wait.
subconclusions.commonsense: State recorded after the wait is worthless for recovering from a crash during the wait, and since the submit call itself takes milliseconds, the only useful ordering is submit-then-record-then-poll.

subconclusions.text: If that write fails (full disk, read-only or wrong-permission cache dir), the job that has already been accepted must carry on rather than aborting, and the failed write has to be reported at warning level rather than swallowed.
subconclusions.commonsense: A cache write is an optimisation for the next run, so its failure should downgrade resumability, not destroy work already paid for, but a silent downgrade is indistinguishable from a bug and has to be announced.

clues_only.reconstruction: The batch id must be written durably into the fingerprint-keyed cache directory under CURATOR_CACHE_DIR the instant submit returns and before polling begins, so any re-run of the identical script resumes the existing job automatically while a changed prompt/model/params/dataset (or a cleared/disabled cache) forces a fresh submission. If that write fails, the paid-for run continues to completion regardless, but the failure must surface as a warning naming the exception and the path rather than being silently swallowed.
constraints: Persist the provider-assigned batch job id to durable storage immediately after the submit call returns and before entering the poll loop — not after the download completes.

The write must land inside the window before the first status/poll response comes back (order of ~200ms–90s), so a re-run started seconds after submit finds the existing job rather than submitting a second one.

Store the batch id in the per-fingerprint cache directory under the cache root (the directory keyed by the hash of prompt function, model name, generation params and dataset), alongside the request and response files — not in the working directory and not in any location outside the cache root.

Resumption must be keyed by the run fingerprint, so that changing the prompt template, model, generation params or dataset yields a different fingerprint and the stale batch id is never picked up for a changed run.
The batch id file must live under CURATOR_CACHE_DIR so a run started on one machine can be resumed on another that shares that path; no part of the resumable state may live somewhere else.

Clearing the cache must remove the stored batch id (it lives in the fingerprint directory), and CURATOR_DISABLE_CACHE must bypass batch-id persistence and resumption cleanly, i.e. a disabled cache means a fresh submission.

A failure to write the batch id (OSError, disk full, permissions on a mounted dir) must not abort or crash the in-flight run: the submission has already been paid for, so catch the error and continue into the poll loop and download the results.

Persistence errors must not be swallowed silently — no bare `except: pass`. Emit a warning-level log that names the exception and includes the full path that could not be written, so a re-run doing all the work again is distinguishable from the cache simply being cold.
When a stored batch id is found for the current fingerprint and the job is still pending, resume polling that job; do not submit a duplicate.
Resumption must be automatic on re-running the same script — no manual step of reading ids from the provider console or pasting them into a scratch script.

Do not add extra hardening around the submit call itself (e.g. pre-submit writes or crash windows there); the failure mode being defended against is death during the wait, not during the ~200ms submit.

Apply the same write-before-you-wait ordering to any other long remote wait introduced later, matching the online processor which appends to the responses file when a request is accepted rather than when it returns.
clues_only.notes: Rule: constraint 1 states persisting the batch job id immediately after submit returns and before the poll loop, and constraint 3 places it in the per-fingerprint cache directory keyed the same way as the prompt cache (hash of prompt fn, model, params, dataset) — matches the rule including the keying and the crash-resumability rationale. with_herrings.reconstruction: The batch id must be persisted the instant the provider accepts the submission — before any polling — into the existing fingerprint-keyed directory under CURATOR_CACHE_DIR alongside requests/responses, so it is cache-clearable, CURATOR_DISABLE_CACHE-respecting, shareable across machines, and immune to false resumes after prompt/model/param/dataset changes. Write failures must never abort a run the user has already paid for, but must surface as a warning naming the path rather than a silent pass, and stale/failed/expired recorded batches must be discarded in favour of a fresh submit.
constraints: Write the batch job record (provider batch id) to disk as soon as the provider accepts the submission and returns the id — before entering the poll loop — rather than waiting for a terminal status.

The write must be synchronous and complete before any status/poll output is produced, so a re-run started seconds after submit (before the first status has come back) already sees the record and does not submit a duplicate.

Do not make the record conditional on terminal/completed status; the earlier 'write on completion' behaviour is superseded because every observed crash happens during the wait, not inside the ~200ms submit call.
Keep the existing completion-time behaviour of writing the reassembled results/responses at terminal status; the new early id write is in addition to it, not a replacement.

Store the record inside the per-run fingerprint directory under the cache root (the same directory that holds the request and response files), not in the working directory and not in an ad-hoc dotfile.

Key the record by the existing run fingerprint (hash of prompt function, model name, generation params and dataset), so changing the prompt, model, params or data yields a different directory and can never resume a batch submitted for different inputs.
The record must live under CURATOR_CACHE_DIR like the request/response files, so a run started on one machine with a shared cache path can be resumed from another machine.
Deleting/clearing the cache directory must remove the batch record too, and CURATOR_DISABLE_CACHE must bypass reading and writing it, with no separate state left behind outside the cache.
If a job is split into several provider batches, append each batch id to the record as that batch is accepted, incrementally, rather than writing the set only after all submissions finish.

A failure to write the record must never abort the run or propagate an exception: catch write errors (disk full/OSError, permissions, read-only or mounted paths) and continue submitting/polling/downloading so the user still gets the results they have already paid for.

Never swallow a failed cache/record write silently with a bare `except: pass`; emit a warning-level log that includes the path that could not be written and makes clear the run continues but the re-run will repeat work.

On resume, if the recorded batch is in a terminal non-success state (failed, expired, cancelled) or is unknown to the provider, discard the record and submit a fresh batch instead of polling a dead job forever.
Resumption must be fully automatic on re-running the same script — no requiring the user to look up batch ids on the provider console or paste them into a scratch script.

Apply the same ordering rule to any other place the code begins a long wait on a remote resource: persist the handle when the remote accepts the work, not after the wait returns (as the online processor already does by appending on request acceptance).
with_herrings.notes: Rule: constraint 1 states the batch id must be written to disk immediately upon provider acceptance, before entering the poll loop; constraints 5-7 place it in the fingerprint-keyed directory under the cache root alongside request/response files, matching 'same keying as the existing prompt cache' and the resume motivation. Scope: submission-time persistence of the batch job id is explicitly the focus, and constraint 4 delimits it from completion-time result writing. Failure behavior: constraint 10 requires write failures never abort the run and processing continue, and constraint 11 requires a warning-level log (not a silent pass) naming the path — both halves present. Extra material (multi-batch append, stale-batch discard, disable-cache) goes beyond the requirement but does not contradict it.

requirement.rule: On restart, before resuming an existing batch job ID, the code must verify the persisted job's provider, model name, and request payload hash still match the current run's configuration; a mismatch must cause a fresh submission rather than resuming a stale/incompatible job.
requirement.failure_behavior: Mismatch causes a fresh submission with a logged reason for why the old job was not resumed, not a silent resume of incompatible results.

subconclusions.text: A persisted batch job may only be picked back up if the provider/backend it was submitted against is the same one the current run is configured for.
subconclusions.commonsense: If resuming under a different backend gives 404 loops and nonsense summaries, then the backend the job was submitted with is part of what makes a stored job reusable.

subconclusions.text: A persisted batch job may only be picked back up if the model name in the current config is the same one the job was submitted with, which means the model has to be recorded alongside the job id.
subconclusions.commonsense: If you can get mini outputs and mini-vs-4o cost figures out of a resume, and nothing on disk says which model the job went out with, the model has to be stored and compared before reuse.

subconclusions.text: A persisted batch job may only be picked back up if the requests the run would send now are the same as the ones the job was submitted with, compared as a hash of the request payloads rather than by run directory or row count.
subconclusions.commonsense: Prompt edits, added rows and changed sampling params all silently survive a resume, so the content of the requests themselves is what has to be compared.

subconclusions.text: When any of those no longer line up, the run submits a brand new batch job and logs why the stored one was not reused, rather than aborting or resuming quietly.
subconclusions.commonsense: Duplicate cost is acceptable and a hard failure is not, so the only remaining option is a fresh submission that says out loud what did not match.

clues_only.reconstruction: Resume-on-restart must be gated by a stored, submit-time fingerprint of the job (model, provider/endpoint, digested request bodies including sampling params, and dataset/request count), with the record keyed per endpoint; any mismatch or unowned/404 job means silently discard and resubmit rather than raise, hang, or blend configs. Every resume or skip must be logged at INFO with the reason, all cost/token/reporting must use the job's actual submitted model rather than the current config, and reassembly must match results by stable request id rather than positional index.
constraints: Resume a pending batch job only if it is equivalent to the job the current script/config would submit right now; on any detected difference, do not reuse it — submit a fresh batch job instead. Correctness of the returned dataset takes priority over the duplicated cost and the 24h turnaround.

The equivalence check must cover the full request bodies, not just prompt text: sampling and generation parameters (e.g. temperature, max_tokens) must be part of the identity. Reuse the same body-digest mechanism already used for the online (non-batch) cache key rather than inventing a weaker batch-only check.
The equivalence check must cover the model name; a config edit from e.g. gpt-4o-mini to gpt-4o must invalidate the pending job.
The equivalence check must cover the provider/backend (openai vs anthropic vs mistral vs gemini); switching backend in the same script must never resume the previous provider's job id.

The equivalence check must cover the concrete endpoint/deployment, distinguishing e.g. plain OpenAI from an Azure deployment of the same model, and the on-disk pending-job record must be keyed by provider/endpoint (not by dataset alone) so two endpoints cannot collide in one slot.

The equivalence check must cover the input dataset contents and request count; appending or editing rows between restarts must invalidate the pending job rather than resuming a job built from the shorter/older set.

The persisted pending-job record must store more than id + request-file path + timestamp: at minimum the model, provider/endpoint, a digest of the request bodies, and the request count, so the resume decision can be made without trusting the current config and so a human handed only a run dir can tell whether resuming is safe.

Do not compare against the request .jsonl currently sitting in the run dir as a proxy for what was submitted — that file is regenerated by the new run; comparison must be against metadata captured at submit time.
A mismatch must never raise, abort or hang the run. The failure mode has to be safe for unattended/nightly jobs: detect, discard the stale job, submit a new one, and keep going.
When a pending job is skipped/discarded, emit an INFO-level line that names the specific field that did not line up (model, provider, endpoint, params, dataset), not just a count of skipped jobs.
When a pending job is resumed, that must also be visible above DEBUG, stating what was matched and the job identity — not just the raw id at DEBUG level.

clues.text: Sanity check on my own build: first line of the task is `print(os.getuid())`. Against the python:3.11-slim I put together for the RAFT verifier it prints 0. Same snippet against the sandbox image we ship prints 1000. Took me an embarrassing while to work out that difference was coming from the image and not from anything I passed.
clues.settles: the team agrees a caller-supplied image currently runs the task as uid 0 while the shipped image does not

carrier.why: The room is already on executor hardening shipping in a hotfix, so a concrete finding that the sandbox image, not the passed params, controls the uid is a direct contribution.

clues.text: Worth remembering the December rebuild before we sign off on the tag work. The appuser line at the bottom of the sandbox Dockerfile got dropped in a refactor and we shipped four days of runs before anybody spotted it. Nothing on our side would ever have noticed. We take whatever the image decided and start it.
clues.settles: the team agrees the executor does not itself decide who the container process runs as

carrier.why: Konrad's recap of a week of back-to-back releases is where a cautionary note about a refactor silently dropping the sandbox appuser line and shipping bad runs reads as release-hygiene rather than a tangent.

clues.text: If we are naming a tag in code anyway, the uid feels like the wrong thing to leave to a Dockerfile. Docker takes a user on the create call and we have simply never passed one.
clues.settles: the team agrees the container user should be an argument the executor passes at create time

carrier.why: The pinning change is in the review queue this week, so proposing that the uid be passed on the create call instead of inherited from a Dockerfile answers the open review question about scope.

clues.text: Lost an afternoon. Pointed `CodeExecutor` at an image of my own so I would stop pip installing pandas per task, and the generated solution decided the tidiest way to pass was to rewrite the input CSV sitting in the mounted dir. Original gone, no backup. On the stock image the same script just errors out when it touches that file.
clues.settles: the team agrees the workspace mount is writable when a custom image is used and not when the shipped one is

carrier.why: The room is verifying that a freshly merged recipe actually runs correctly, which is exactly where Dario's story of a custom image letting generated code clobber the input file belongs.

clues.text: Half the reason the workspace bind is set up the way it is: a model solution physically cannot edit the test file, so grading means something. Ran last week's batch on a custom image someone handed me and three solutions passed by overwriting the assertions. I only caught it because the pass rate jumped.
clues.settles: the team agrees write protection on the mount is what makes verifier results trustworthy and it was absent on a custom image

carrier.why: Nikolai's own verifier work is on the table here, so evidence that a custom image let solutions overwrite the test assertions is the argument for why the pending change matters to him.

clues.text: On the thread with the team who want their own image: they want it purely so scipy and their internal client lib are already there, they are not asking us to change how the container runs. I told them the workspace still comes in read-only from our side and they said fine, they write everything to stdout anyway.
clues.settles: the team agrees a caller-supplied image is expected to keep the write-protected workspace

carrier.why: This is the working thread on the override, and the concrete requirement from the team asking for their own image settles what the override actually has to allow.

clues.text: Got asked at the demo whether the sandbox guarantees still hold if you bring your own image. I said "should do", then went and checked afterwards, and now I would like to un-say it.
clues.settles: the team agrees the sandbox properties do not currently survive a caller-supplied image

carrier.why: The room is deciding whether long-stale PRs still matter, and a demo question he answered wrongly is the clearest reason to move this one now.

clues.text: Pinning the tag is a reproducibility fix. Whether the container is locked down is a different axis and I do not want it riding on which tag you happen to get handed.
clues.settles: the team agrees the container's protections must not be a side effect of using the default tag

carrier.why: The channel is already checking that two landing changes do not entangle, so Dermot's insistence that reproducibility and container lockdown stay separate axes is on-topic.

clues.text: Reading the docker backend before I review this: when a caller sets `backend_params={'image': ...}` the create call goes down a shorter path than the default one, and the extra kwargs we assemble for our own tag never get near it. I do not think anybody chose that, it is just where the code ended up.
clues.settles: the team agrees the override path skips the container settings the default path applies

carrier.why: He is reviewing the pinning change in this very thread, and the discovery that the override path bypasses the assembled kwargs is the code-level answer the thread needs.

clues.text: Follow-up on my image mess: the entrypoint does an apt-get at container start, which is why it wanted to be root. The batch ran to completion, the numbers looked normal, and I only found out days later because I opened the Dockerfile for an unrelated reason. Nothing anywhere told me the run had been different from every other run.
clues.settles: the team agrees a run whose image needed root completed with no indication anything was different

carrier.why: The room is reviewing request-processing architecture and what gets surfaced, so the complaint that nothing recorded the run being different lands as an observability gap.

clues.text: Heads up from the CLI side: when a docker task dies at container start, all the progress table gets is the task marked failed plus a container id. People screenshot it and send it to me and I have nothing to tell them. If we are going to start having creates rejected, whatever text comes back needs to name the setting that was rejected or it lands in my inbox instead.
clues.settles: the team agrees a startup rejection has to surface a message naming what was rejected

carrier.why: They are already discussing how an exception comes out mangled under the progress display, so Gideon's demand that rejection text name the offending setting is the same conversation.

clues.text: If we do tighten this, my preference is the first task blows up at create.
clues.settles: the team agrees an incompatible image should stop the run at container start rather than continue

carrier.why: The thread is opening the question of how strict to be, and his preference for failing loudly at the first create rather than mid-batch answers it directly.
